newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Tasmania shooting accused to get fair trial-lawyer.
newsitem.headline: Tasmania shooting accused to get fair trial-lawyer.

text.p: The lawyer defending the man charged with the worst mass murder in modern Australian history expressed confidence on Friday that his client would receive a fair trial from an impartial jury next month.

John Avery, who agreed to represent Martin Bryant after his previous lawyer quit this week, also told the Supreme Court in the southern state of Tasmania that he saw no need to delay the November 19 trial.
Bryant, 29, did not appear for Friday's brief pre-trial hearing and remained in his maximum-security cell in the hospital wing of Hobart's Risdon prison.
Bryant on Monday pleaded not guilty to 35 charges of murder and 37 lesser charges, including counts of attempted murder, wounding and arson.
"There is no risk that I won't be ready to proceed," Avery told the court in the island state's capital on Friday.
He later said he was confident Bryant could expect a fair trial and that he had no concerns about the prospect of finding an impartial jury to try the case.
Avery did not give any indication of the basis for Bryant's not-guilty pleas.
Bryant has been the subject of numerous death threats. Tasmanian bomb squad police combed the Supreme Court building in Hobart before his 25-minute appearance on Monday.
On April 28, a sunny Sunday afternoon, a lone gunman walked into the Broad Arrow Cafe at the popular Port Arthur tourist site and shot 20 people at they ate their lunch.
Within an hour, a further 12 people, including a three-year-old girl, were gunned down either outside the cafe, in their cars, or hiding behind a tree.
Three other people were taken hostage and later found dead in the charred remains of the nearby Seascape guest house.
Legislation that would strip Bryant of his wealth if he is convicted, was brought before the Tasmanian parliament this week.
Tasmanian Attorney-General Ray Groom, who drafted the Criminal Injuries Compensation Amendment Bill soon after the shootings, has valued Bryant's assets at up to A$1.5 million (US$1.2 million).
No reason has been given for why Bryant's former laywer, barrister David Gunson, quit the case. But Avery told reporters on Friday that Bryant had asked him to be his new counsel.
Avery met Bryant in his prison cell on Thursday but declined to comment on his client's condition.
Asked if Bryant might change his pleas before the trial, Avery said: "There was no indication of that."
